name: One wall knocked through
brief:
A fire crew crosses a building plan from `S` to `E`. The plan is `grid`, a list of equal-length strings: `#` is a wall, and every other cell is floor. Each move goes to the cell above, below, left or right. The crew may knock through at most one wall cell, which then counts as floor. Return the fewest moves from `S` to `E`, or `-1` when even one knocked-through wall cannot join them.

Write `fewest_moves_one_break(grid)`.

Example. In `['S.#.', '###.', 'E#..']` the walls shut `S` in with one floor cell, and `E` sits alone. Knocking through the wall below `S` gives a route of 2 moves, so the answer is 2.
constraints: At most $300$ rows and $300$ columns; `S` and `E` each appear once.
$O(\text{rows} \times \text{cols})$ time is the target. Knocking through each wall in turn and searching again is too slow.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: Search from `S` and from `E` once each. A route through wall cell `w` costs the nearest `S`-side neighbour of `w`, plus the nearest `E`-side neighbour, plus 2. Compare the best of these with the route that knocks nothing down.

examples.note: Knocking through the wall below `S` joins it to `E` in 2 moves.
The open route takes 5 moves, and no single wall makes it shorter.
Every wall beside `S` has only walls beyond it, so one knock is not enough.

tests.call: fewest_moves_one_break([''.join('S' if (i, j) == (0, 0) else 'E' if (i, j) == (299, 299) else '#' if ((i * 2654435761 + j * 40503) >> 7) % 10 < 3 else '.' for j in range(300)) for i in range(300)])
fewest_moves_one_break([''.join('S' if (i, j) == (0, 0) else 'E' if (i, j) == (0, 299) else '#' if j % 3 == 1 and (i + j) % 211 else '.' for j in range(300)) for i in range(300)])

how: Submit runs 14 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value. The obvious method knocks through each wall cell in turn and searches again, which is a full search for every wall and runs out of time on the large plans. The step to the target is two searches, one from each end, after which each wall is priced from its neighbours in $O(1)$. Unlike the version that allows several knocks, exactly one is allowed, which is what lets each wall be priced from two searches.
notes: A route through one wall is a shortest walk from `S` to a neighbour of the wall, two moves through it, and a shortest walk on to `E`.
The route that knocks nothing down must be compared too, and a wall counts only when it has a neighbour reached from each end.
Two searches and one pass over the walls make the work $O(\text{rows} \times \text{cols})$.

planted.slip: Marking a cell seen once, whatever the knock state, lets a route that spent its knock block a route that still has one.
Pricing only the routes through a wall forgets the route that needs no knock at all.
Knocking through each wall in turn and searching again is right but repeats a full search for every wall, too slow on the large plans.
